[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain why the sky is blue but sunsets are red, properly, not the one-line version."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Both come out of the same mechanism - Rayleigh scattering - looked at from two different geometries.

Air molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and in that regime the scattering efficiency goes as one over wavelength to the fourth power. Blue light at 450 nanometres is scattered roughly five times more strongly than red at 700. So when you look at any part of the sky away from the sun, what reaches your eye is sunlight that has been redirected toward you, and that redirected light is overwhelmingly the blue end.

Why not violet, which scatters even more? Two reasons: the sun emits less violet than blue, and human cone sensitivity falls off sharply at the violet end. The physics does produce more violet; your eye largely doesn't report it.

Sunsets are the complementary view. Near the horizon the light travels through perhaps forty times as much atmosphere as it does overhead. By the time it reaches you, the blue has been scattered out of the beam almost completely - scattered sideways, into somebody else's sky - and what survives the journey along that path is the red and orange that scatter least. You are seeing the leftovers."}, {"role": "user", "content": "So why are clouds white and not blue?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Because cloud droplets are the wrong size for Rayleigh scattering, and size is the whole story here.

Rayleigh scattering applies when the scatterer is much smaller than the wavelength - air molecules are about 0.3 nanometres against 500 nanometre light. Cloud droplets are 10 to 20 micrometres, which is twenty to forty times *larger* than the wavelength. That puts them in the Mie regime, where the scattering efficiency is essentially independent of wavelength.

So a cloud scatters red, green and blue equally well, and equal parts of all visible wavelengths is what white means.

The same reasoning explains a few other everyday things. Fog is white for the identical reason. Milk is white because the fat globules are also micron-scale. And the deep grey of a rain cloud isn't a different colour at all - it's the same white scattering, with so much depth of droplets above you that most of the light gets scattered back out of the top before it reaches the bottom."}]

You get a reliable byte stream and you pay for it in latency and in head-of-line blocking: if packet 5 is lost, packets 6 through 20 sit in a buffer waiting for it even though they arrived fine.

UDP does none of that. It sends a datagram with a length and a checksum and forgets about it. No ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control unless you write it yourself.

You pick UDP when late data is worse than missing data. Voice and video are the clearest case: a 200 millisecond old audio frame is useless, so retransmitting it actively hurts - you would rather conceal the gap and stay current. Games are the same argument with position updates. DNS uses it because a query and a reply fit in one packet each and setting up a connection would double the round trips for no benefit.

The interesting modern case is QUIC, which runs over UDP and then rebuilds reliability, ordering and congestion control on top - specifically so it can avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking across independent streams, and so it can be updated without waiting for operating system kernels to change."}, {"role": "user", "content": "So is QUIC just TCP with extra steps?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's a fair suspicion, and the answer is no, for three reasons that each turned out to matter more than people expected.

On a mobile connection where a round trip is 80 milliseconds, that is the difference people actually feel.

It lives in userspace. TCP is implemented in the kernel, so improvements ship on the operating system's schedule, which is measured in years. QUIC ships with the browser and the server, so congestion control changes roll out in weeks.
